---
title: "Farrington"
---

The RKI chapter judged a week by averaging a handful of comparable weeks.
Farrington asks the same question — is this week high *for this week of the
year* — but answers it by fitting a model to those weeks instead of averaging
them. A regression line gives a baseline that can rise or fall over the years,
one shared dispersion parameter says how much ordinary weeks scatter around it,
and a right-skewed prediction interval supplies the threshold.

That buys one thing a reference set cannot: the method can notice that some of
its own reference weeks were themselves epidemic, and discount them. How harshly
it should discount them is the question the whole method turns on, and the two
published versions answer it differently.

The method comes from the Communicable Disease Surveillance Centre in England and
Wales, where it was built to screen weekly laboratory reports across more than
three thousand organisms at once [@farrington1996]. That setting shaped it: one
formula, no per-disease tuning, working equally on an organism seen a few times a
year and one seen hundreds of times a week. Noufaily and colleagues revised it
seventeen years later after simulation showed the false alarm rate was too high
[@noufaily2013].

## Which weeks count as comparable {#sec-farr-reference}

Both versions start from the same window. For the week under assessment, take
the same calendar week in each of the $b$ previous years, plus $w$ weeks either
side:

$$
R \;=\; \bigl\{\, t_0 - 52i + j \;:\; i = 1,\dots,b;\ j = -w,\dots,+w \,\bigr\}, \qquad n = b(2w+1).
$$

With the package defaults $b = 5$ and $w = 3$, that is 35 weeks. Seasonality is
handled by the choice of window rather than by a term in the model: only weeks
sitting at the same point in the year are ever compared, so no sine and cosine
are needed. The current year is excluded, so an outbreak in progress cannot
inflate its own baseline.

The cost is visible as soon as you draw it.

::: {#fig-farr-reference}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-farr-reference"></div>
```

Which weeks each version lets the regression see. Switch between the two
versions and change $b$ and $w$.
:::

Thirty-five weeks out of the 260 in five years is 13% of the data. The other 87%
is not merely unused for the baseline — it is unavailable for estimating the
trend and the dispersion too, which is where a thin reference set hurts most.

The 2013 revision keeps the window but stops discarding everything else. It adds
a **ten-level seasonal factor**: the window itself is the reference level, and
the remaining weeks of the year are divided into nine blocks, which fit exactly
since $7 + 9 \times 5 = 52$. Each block gets its own multiplier $e^{\delta_j}$.
Weeks outside the window are now *explained* by their block rather than thrown
away, so they contribute to $\beta$ and $\varphi$ without dragging the current
window's level around.

Two further changes come with it. The 26 weeks immediately before $t_0$ are held
out, so a new outbreak a few weeks old cannot teach the model to expect itself —
the 1996 version needed no such rule, because its windows already sat the better
part of a year away. The arithmetic gives

$$ n = 52b + w - 26 = 237 $$

reference weeks at the defaults, against 35. The third change comes free with
it: with 200-odd points behind the slope, the trend no longer has to pass a
significance test to be kept [@noufaily2013].

## Computing an epidemic threshold with Farrington {#sec-farr-threshold}

::: {.algo-step}
**1. Fit a quasi-Poisson regression.** On the reference counts,

$$ \log \mu_i = \alpha + \beta t_i, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(y_i) = \varphi\,\mu_i. $$

Here $\alpha$ is the baseline level on the log scale and $\beta$ the weekly
change, so $e^{\beta}$ is a weekly multiplier. The quasi-Poisson family is there
because surveillance counts are almost always overdispersed; @sec-rki-dispersion
sets out what happens when that is ignored. In the 2013 version the seasonal
factor joins the linear predictor as $\log \mu_i = \theta + \beta t_i + \delta_{j(i)}$.
:::

::: {.algo-step}
**2. Estimate the dispersion, with a floor at 1.** From the weighted Pearson
statistic,

$$ \varphi = \max\left\{1,\; \frac{1}{n-p}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \omega_i \frac{(y_i - \mu_i)^2}{\mu_i}\right\}, $$

where $p$ is the number of regression parameters and $\omega_i = 1$ on the first
pass. The floor matters: $\varphi < 1$ would mean "less variable than Poisson",
which on 35 points is nearly always estimation noise, so Poisson variance is
taken as the minimum.
:::

::: {.algo-step}
**3. Downweight the weeks that look like past outbreaks.** For each reference
week compute a standardised Anscombe residual,

$$ s_i \;=\; \frac{y_i^{2/3} - \mu_i^{2/3}}{\tfrac{2}{3}\sqrt{\varphi}\;\mu_i^{1/6}\sqrt{1 - h_{ii}}}, $$

then assign weights and fit once more:

$$
\omega_i =
\begin{cases}
\gamma / s_i^2, & s_i > c,\\
\gamma, & s_i \le c,
\end{cases}
\qquad \gamma \text{ chosen so that } \textstyle\sum_i \omega_i = n.
$$

The cut-off is $c = 1$ in 1996 and $c = 2.58$ in 2013 [@noufaily2013].
:::

::: {.algo-step}
**4. Keep the trend only if it is worth keeping.** The $\beta t$ term survives
when $\beta$ is significant at 5%, when the predicted $\mu_0$ does not exceed the
largest count in the reference set, and (in the R implementation) when
$b \ge 3$. Otherwise the whole procedure is repeated with an intercept-only
model. A trend estimated from $b$ clusters a year apart and then extrapolated a
further year can blow $\mu_0$ up exponentially, which is what the second
condition guards against. In 2013 the significance test is dropped — with 200-odd
points the slope is stable enough — but both safety catches remain.
:::

::: {.algo-step}
**5. Take the upper end of the prediction interval.** Two things are uncertain:
the count itself, with variance $\varphi\mu_0$, and the estimated mean, with
variance $\operatorname{Var}(\mu_0)$. The 1996 threshold adds them on the $2/3$
power scale, where a Poisson count is close to symmetric:

$$ U = \mu_0\left(1 + \frac{2}{3}\,z\,\sqrt{\frac{\varphi\mu_0 + \operatorname{Var}(\mu_0)}{\mu_0^{2}}}\,\right)^{3/2}. $$

The 2013 threshold instead reads a quantile straight off a negative binomial with
the same mean and variance:

$$ U = F^{-1}_{\mathrm{NB}}\!\left(1-\alpha;\ \text{size} = \frac{\mu_0}{\varphi - 1},\ \text{prob} = \frac{1}{\varphi}\right). $$
:::

::: {.algo-step}
**6. Score it, and refuse to alarm on almost nothing.** The result is reported as
an exceedance score,

$$ X = \frac{y_0 - \mu_0}{U - \mu_0}, $$

which is dimensionless: $X < 1$ is inside the interval, $X = 1$ sits exactly on
the threshold, $X = 2$ is twice as far past expectation as it needed to be. A
rare organism at 9 cases against 2 expected and a common one at 520 against 400
can be ranked on the same scale. Finally, a rule of thumb against alarms on
near-empty series: **no alarm unless there are at least 5 cases in the last 4
weeks**.
:::

### Reading the threshold formula {#sec-farr-reading}

The 1996 expression is easier to trust once unpacked. Work on the scale
$y^{2/3}$, where the right skew of a Poisson count largely disappears. On that
scale the standard deviation of the prediction error is
$\tfrac{2}{3}\mu_0^{1/6}\sqrt{\tau}$, with

$$ \tau = \varphi + \frac{\operatorname{Var}(\mu_0)}{\mu_0}. $$

Add $z$ of them to $\mu_0^{2/3}$ and raise the result back to the power $3/2$:

$$ U = \left(\mu_0^{2/3} + z\,\tfrac{2}{3}\,\mu_0^{1/6}\sqrt{\tau}\right)^{3/2}. $$

That is the same formula as above, and it is line for line what the package
computes.

Which parts of it actually matter is worth knowing before tuning anything. Take
$\mu_0 = 10$, $\varphi = 1.5$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\mu_0) = 0.5$:

| | $U$ |
|---|---:|
| $z = 1.645$ (one-sided 5%, the `farringtonFlexible` default) | 17.13 |
| $z = 1.96$ (two-sided 5%, the `algo.farrington` default) | 18.64 |
| $z = 2.58$ (one-sided 0.5%, used by UKHSA) | 21.72 |
| at $z=1.96$, dropping $\operatorname{Var}(\mu_0)$ entirely | 18.48 |
| at $z=1.96$, with $\varphi = 1$ instead of 1.5 | 16.98 |
| at $z=1.96$, with $\varphi = 3$ instead of 1.5 | 22.59 |

: What moves the threshold, at a fixed expected count of 10 cases.
{#tbl-farr-sensitivity}

Ignoring the uncertainty in the mean altogether costs about a sixth of a case.
Changing $\varphi$ from 1 to 3 moves the threshold by five and a half.
**$\varphi$ and $z$ are what set the distance between expectation and
threshold**; the delta-method refinement is a rounding detail beside them.

For the same numbers the negative binomial rule gives $U = 17$, against 17.13
from the $2/3$ formula — the two threshold rules agree closely. They differ in
kind rather than in value: the NB quantile is always a whole number and needs no
back transformation, which is what matters on sparse series, but it plugs
$\mu_0$ and $\varphi$ straight in and ignores their uncertainty.

## The cut-off that decides how much history to believe {#sec-farr-reweight}

Step 3 is where the two versions actually part company, and the reason is a piece
of arithmetic the 1996 authors did not have in front of them.

If nothing is wrong, the standardised residuals are roughly standard normal. So a
cut-off of 1 catches about **16% of perfectly ordinary weeks** and shrinks them.
The weeks it shrinks hardest are the ones with the largest squared residuals —
precisely the ones carrying the information about how much ordinary weeks
scatter. The result is that $\varphi$ is pulled down, often onto its own floor of
1, the threshold follows it down, and false alarms go up. Raising the cut-off to
2.58 leaves about 0.5% of ordinary weeks affected, so only something genuinely
extreme is discounted.

::: {#fig-farr-reweight}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-farr-reweight"></div>
```

Thirty-five reference weeks, one year of which carried an outbreak through the
window. Hollow circles are downweighted, with the factor applied. The grey line
is the fit with no downweighting at all.
:::

The figure holds the data fixed and moves only the cut-off, and the three regimes
come out clearly. Turn reweighting off and the old outbreak counts in full:
$\varphi$ stays at 2.05, the threshold rises to 16.3, and a new outbreak would
have to be very large to clear it. Set the cut-off to 1 and three of the 35 weeks
are shrunk, $\varphi$ collapses onto its floor of 1.00, and the threshold drops
to 12.89. Set it to 2.58 and only the single most extreme week is touched,
$\varphi$ settles at 1.28, and the threshold lands at 14.12.

The week being assessed notified 13 cases. Under the 1996 cut-off that is an
alarm; under the 2013 cut-off it is not. Same data, same formula, same week —
one parameter.

Two properties of the weighting rule are easy to miss. It is **one-sided**: a
week that is unusually *low* keeps its full weight, which makes this a filter for
past outbreaks rather than robust regression in general. And $\gamma$ does not
move the fitted line at all; it exists only to keep the weights averaging 1, so
that the $n - p$ denominator in step 2 still means something.

## What the revision bought {#sec-farr-evidence}

| | 1996 | 2013 |
|---|---|---|
| Reference weeks ($b=5$, $w=3$) | 35 | about 237 |
| Seasonality | by choice of window | window plus a 10-level factor |
| Recent weeks excluded | $w$ | 26 |
| Trend | kept if $p < 0.05$ | always kept |
| Anscombe cut-off | 1 | 2.58 |
| Threshold | normal approximation, $2/3$ scale | negative binomial quantile |

: The five changes. The low-count rule and the exceedance score are unchanged.
{#tbl-farr-versions}

An evaluation by the same group across 959 disease series puts numbers on the
trade: the false alarm rate fell from **1.63%** to **0.76%** for the negative
binomial version and 0.87% for the quasi-Poisson one, while the probability of
detection fell from **57%** to 51% and 53% respectively [@enki2016]. Public
Health England moved to the negative binomial version. Read the two rows
together: roughly half the false alarms, at the cost of a few points of
sensitivity — a less flattering picture than "without reducing sensitivity", and
the honest one to quote.

## Running it {#sec-farr-package}

`farringtonFlexible()` in R's `surveillance` package runs either version
depending on the `control` list [@salmon2016]. Three things about it cause
trouble.

**The defaults are neither version.** They take the reference set, the trend test
and the threshold formula from 1996, but the weight cut-off 2.58 from 2013. For
the 2013 method you have to ask for it:

```r
control <- list(range = weeks,
                b = 5, w = 3,
                noPeriods = 10,              # the seasonal factor
                pastWeeksNotIncluded = 26,
                pThresholdTrend = 1,         # always keep the trend
                weightsThreshold = 2.58,
                thresholdMethod = "nbPlugin",
                alpha = 0.05)                # one-sided here
res <- farringtonFlexible(sts_object, control)
```

**`alpha` means different things in different functions.** `algo.farrington()`
uses `qnorm(1 - alpha/2)`, two-sided; `farringtonFlexible()` uses the
$1-\alpha$ quantile, one-sided. At the same nominal `alpha` the newer function
sets a lower threshold and raises more alarms, and comparing the two means
doubling `alpha` for one of them.

**Misspelled names in `control` are ignored in silence.** There is no error and
no warning; the run simply uses the default. Check the returned object rather
than assuming the setting took.

Two more things worth knowing before building a pipeline on it. The earliest week
that can be assessed is $52b + w + 1$, so five years of history buys you nothing
until week 264. And weeks failing the 5-in-4 rule come back with
`upperbound = NA`, which breaks the threshold line into pieces on sparse series —
decide in advance whether to relax the rule or aggregate the units.

## What an alarm is, and is not {#sec-farr-interpretation}

A Farrington alarm says one thing: this week's count is higher than a model
fitted to comparable weeks in the past predicted, at the chosen error rate.
ECDC's own documentation for the method states plainly that such signals "do not
necessarily correspond to outbreaks", and are there to triage many series
efficiently [@ecdc_signal].

Every agency running it pairs it with filters and with people. UKHSA sets
$\alpha = 0.005$. France's food-chain *Salmonella* system keeps only signals that
three algorithms agree on, or that persist beyond two weeks. The reason is
arithmetic rather than caution: at a one-sided $\alpha = 0.05$ with a correct
model, each series crosses its threshold by chance about one week in twenty, so
**168 wards monitored at that level produce roughly eight chance signals every
week**. That is the same multiple-comparisons problem as @sec-bayes-practice, and
it does not care which algorithm raised the signal.

Three structural limits are worth stating alongside the method, because they
follow from its shape rather than from any implementation.

It **judges each week alone**. There is no accumulation of evidence, so a rise
that is small but sustained can pass without any single week clearing the
threshold. That is exactly the gap CUSUM fills, and the package's own
documentation suggests pairing the two.

It **assumes the season has the same shape every year**. The seasonal factor is
estimated from past years and applied to this one, so a season arriving early or
late is compared against the wrong step.

It has **nowhere to put a covariate**. Temperature, rainfall and population
movement cannot enter the model, which is the limitation the Bayesian chapter
addresses directly.

One more thing it does not do, which is easy to expect of it. A normal seasonal
rise is not an alarm. The method answers "is this week unusual *for this time of
year*", not "has the season started". For the second question you need a
different tool.
